name: Design an Online Presence Service
intent: Show which friends are online, away or typing for hundreds of millions of users on several devices each, without drowning the system in heartbeats and status messages.
codeTitle: heartbeats with a TTL, sessions per device, and fan-out only on change
finalIntro: One user coming online on a phone, opening a laptop, and later going away.
prompt: Design the presence feature of a chat app with 500 million users. Each user sees a green dot next to friends who are online, a 'last seen' time for those who are not, and a 'typing...' indicator inside a conversation. Users are signed in on a phone, a laptop and sometimes a tablet at once, and phones lose their connection all the time.
functional: Show whether each friend is online or offline, and when they were last seen
Treat a user as online if any of their devices is connected
Show 'typing...' to the other people in a conversation
Let a user appear offline or away on purpose
Tell the people who are looking when a friend's status changes
nonFunctional: A status change reaches interested friends within a few seconds
A crashed or disconnected device is noticed within about 30 seconds without any goodbye message
Tens of millions of users are connected at the peak, each sending a heartbeat every 30 seconds
A brief network blip must not make a user flicker offline and back online
Presence may be slightly stale, but it must heal itself and never stay wrong for long
A mass reconnect after an outage must not take the service down again

firstAttempt.text: One SQL table: user id, status and last_seen. Each client sends 'I am here' every few seconds, and the server updates the row. A cron job marks users offline when last_seen is too old. A client shows a friend list by querying the rows of all its friends, and refreshes every few seconds.
limits: Millions of heartbeats per second become millions of row updates per second on one table
Polling by every client turns the friend list into a flood of reads for rows that rarely change
A user on two devices is overwritten by whichever device last wrote, so one device going offline hides the other
The cron job marks users offline late and in big bursts, and a crashed phone looks online for minutes
There is no way to tell friends about a change, and typing indicators are far too fast for a database

steps.title: Use heartbeats and a key that expires
steps.problem: A phone that loses signal or dies cannot say goodbye, so 'offline' cannot depend on a message the device sends. And a database row per user cannot absorb millions of writes per second.
steps.fix: Clients hold a connection to a gateway and send a small heartbeat every 10 to 30 seconds. Each heartbeat renews a key in an in-memory store with a time to live of about three heartbeat intervals. If the key is still there, the user is online. If heartbeats stop, the key expires by itself and the user becomes offline without anyone having to notice. Missed beats are tolerated, because one or two lost packets do not reach the TTL.
steps.tradeoff: Crashes are detected automatically and the write is one cheap in-memory operation. Detection is never instant, since it takes up to the TTL, and a short TTL detects faster but flickers on a bad network, while a long TTL is steady but slow to notice that someone left.

steps.title: Track each device session, and derive the user
steps.problem: A user is on a phone and a laptop. If presence is one value per user, the phone going to sleep makes the user look offline while they are typing on the laptop.
steps.fix: The key is per session (user and device), not per user. A presence service counts the live sessions of each user: the first session makes the user online, and only the loss of the last one makes them offline. The status is the best across devices, so active beats idle beats offline. Each session carries the gateway and device it lives on, which is also how a message finds the right connection.
steps.tradeoff: The status is correct with any number of devices, and a single device can be dropped and re-added safely. There are several keys per user, and the count needs care: a lost expiry or a race between two sessions can leave a count wrong, so it is recomputed from the keys, which are the truth, rather than kept as a separate counter.

steps.title: Publish changes only, and fan out to interested friends
steps.problem: If every heartbeat were sent to every friend, 2.5 million heartbeats per second times hundreds of friends would be an impossible load, and almost all of it would say 'still online'.
steps.fix: Heartbeats never leave the presence service. Only a change of status (offline to online, online to offline, or a manual away) is published to a stream. Fan-out workers read the user's friend list and send the change to friends who are connected and currently looking at that user, such as an open contact list or conversation, rather than to all hundreds of friends. A client that opens a screen subscribes to its visible users and gets their current status at once.
steps.tradeoff: Traffic is proportional to changes, which are rare, instead of heartbeats, and offline friends cost nothing. A popular user with millions of followers is a very large fan-out, and subscribing to only what is on screen adds some bookkeeping on every scroll.

steps.title: Send typing indicators as ephemeral events
steps.problem: 'Typing...' changes every second or two and only matters to the one other person, so it is too fast and too small to deserve storage or fan-out to a whole friend list.
steps.fix: A typing event goes from the client over its connection to a relay, which forwards it straight to the other members' connections in that conversation. Nothing is stored. The sender repeats it at most every few seconds while the user types, and the receiving app hides the indicator after about 5 seconds without a refresh, so a lost 'stopped typing' message cannot leave it stuck. Group chats are capped, and in very large channels the indicator is dropped or sampled.
steps.tradeoff: It is very cheap, and a missed event only means the indicator is a little late. It is best effort and can be missed on a flaky connection, so nothing that matters can depend on it, and without a cap on events per user a client could flood a room.

steps.title: Survive a mass reconnect
steps.problem: When a gateway fails or a network recovers, millions of clients reconnect in the same moment. Each reconnect writes sessions, flips statuses and fans out, so the recovery itself can knock the service down again.
steps.fix: Clients reconnect with exponential backoff and random jitter, so that arrivals spread over many seconds instead of one. A reconnect throttle in front of the gateways admits connections at a rate the backend can take and tells the rest to retry later. After a gateway failure, the presence service does not publish a wave of offline events immediately: sessions simply get a grace period of one TTL, and clients that reconnect to another gateway renew their keys before they would have expired. Extra gateways can be added by autoscaling as load grows.
steps.tradeoff: The recovery is smooth and the backend stays within its limits. Some users wait a few extra seconds to be connected, and during the grace period a user who really left looks online a little longer.

steps.title: Accept approximate presence where exactness is not worth it
steps.problem: Being exactly right everywhere costs a great deal, and nobody can tell whether a friend came online 3 seconds ago or 8 seconds ago. Some cases, such as a channel with a million members, cannot afford per-person updates at all.
steps.fix: Presence is eventually consistent by design. Reads come from a cache that is updated by the fan-out stream and refreshed by a short TTL, so a late update fixes itself. Large groups show only a count, such as '12,400 online', refreshed every few seconds, or the presence of a small sample, instead of an individual dot for each member. 'Last seen' is rounded to a coarse time, and may be written no more than once a minute.
steps.tradeoff: Cost drops by orders of magnitude and the system stays simple to scale. A friend can appear online for a few seconds after leaving, and anything that needs an exact answer, such as deciding whether to send a push notification, should check the live sessions directly rather than rely on the cached dot.

failures.scenario: A phone goes through a tunnel and misses three heartbeats
failures.impact: With a TTL equal to one interval, the user flickers offline and back, and every friend gets two notifications.
failures.answer: The TTL is set to about three intervals, so a couple of lost heartbeats do not expire the session. Clients also resend on reconnect, and the presence service can wait a few seconds before publishing 'offline' so that a quick return cancels the change.

failures.scenario: A gateway machine crashes with 200,000 connections on it
failures.impact: All of those sessions stop renewing at once, and without care a flood of offline events and reconnects would follow.
failures.answer: Clients reconnect to other gateways with jittered backoff and renew their keys. Sessions that do not come back expire after the TTL, and only then do their users go offline. The throttle keeps the reconnect rate within what the backend takes.

failures.scenario: The presence store loses a shard
failures.impact: Thousands of sessions vanish, so users look offline although they are connected.
failures.answer: A replica takes over, and connected clients notice nothing and renew their sessions with the next heartbeat, which rebuilds the lost state within one interval. Statuses are therefore wrong for about 10 to 30 seconds at worst, and nothing needs to be restored from a backup.

failures.scenario: A celebrity with 20 million followers comes online
failures.impact: One status change would become 20 million messages in the same second.
failures.answer: Fan-out reaches only followers who are connected and watching, and large accounts are handled with a lazy, pull-based path: followers see the status when they open the profile, from the cache. Updates are batched and spread over a few seconds, and celebrities are not shown a live dot at all.

alternatives.title: How to detect that a user left

options.name: Heartbeat with a TTL
options.pro: Handles crashes and lost networks, and needs nothing from the dying client
options.con: Detection is delayed by up to the TTL, and heartbeats cost traffic

options.name: Connection close events
options.pro: Instant when a connection closes cleanly
options.con: Half-open connections can stay for minutes, and a failed machine reports nothing

options.name: Both together
options.pro: Instant when the close is seen, and the TTL is the safety net
options.con: Two sources of truth to reconcile

alternatives.pick: Use a TTL as the truth, and treat a clean close as a hint that lets the user go offline sooner.

alternatives.title: How to tell friends

options.name: Clients poll
options.pro: Simple, with nothing to keep on the server
options.con: Wasteful, slow, and enormous for hundreds of millions of users

options.name: Push on change to those watching
options.pro: Traffic follows real changes and real viewers
options.con: Needs subscriptions and a fan-out service

options.name: Push every change to every friend
options.pro: Nothing to track on the client
options.con: Most of the messages go to people who are not looking

alternatives.pick: Push changes to friends who are watching, with a fetch from the cache when a screen opens.

alternatives.title: Where presence is kept

options.name: Relational database
options.con: Presence is high-churn and disposable, so durability buys nothing

options.name: In-memory store with TTL keys
options.pro: Fast, with expiry built in, and it rebuilds from the next heartbeats
options.con: Memory-bound and it forgets on a crash, which is acceptable here

options.name: State held in the gateway
options.con: Other services cannot see it, and it is lost with the machine

alternatives.pick: A sharded in-memory store with TTL keys, rebuilt from heartbeats.

alternatives.title: How exact presence should be

options.name: Exact for everyone
options.con: Costs a message per change for every observer, and it still lags the network anyway

options.name: Approximate, within a few seconds
options.pro: Cheap, caches well, and heals by itself
options.con: A friend can look online for a moment after leaving

options.name: Counts for big groups
options.pro: Constant cost however large the room

alternatives.pick: Approximate by default, with counts for large groups, and exact checks only for decisions such as notifications.
